title: Epicurus - Proto-Scientist, Secular-Saint, and Sophisticated Hedonist
author: Jacob Bell
summary: Published by Classical Wisdom, this essay by Jacob Bell sets out to rescue Epicurus from the modern caricature that links his name to excess, drinking and food apps. Bell argues that the Hellenistic philosopher in fact preached moderation, a reduction of desires and a simple life shared with friends in his garden school. Epicurean hedonism is presented as a sophisticated calculation of lasting contentment and the absence of pain, with friendship ranked as the highest human relationship. The essay also shows how Epicurus's atomistic physics and denial of an immaterial soul or meddling gods served his ethical aim, which was to free people from the fear of divine punishment and of death. A short editor's introduction by Anya Leonard frames the piece with a light-hearted aside about Brazilian culture. The result is an accessible primer on a philosophy of happiness that belongs in any classical reading list.
points: Epicurus is widely misunderstood: his philosophy of pleasure was an ethic of moderation, simple living and cheerfulness, not indulgence.
Choosing the best pleasure means looking ahead to what brings sustaining contentment and the absence of pain, which is why Epicureans moderate wine and visit the dentist.
Friendship ranked above even family in Epicurus's scheme because it supplies security, tranquility and pleasure, and he warned that the race for wealth, fame and power destroys peace.
His atomistic physics was never pursued for its own sake: it served the ethical goal of removing the anxiety created by meddling gods, an immortal soul and fear of punishment after death.
The argument that death is nothing to us because what is dissolved has no sensation remains one of the most quoted consolations in ancient philosophy.
quotes: There is probably no other ancient Greek philosopher who has been so misunderstood in our modern era. Nowadays his philosophy is associated with excess and drinking and food apps… but the reality is, he preached the exact opposite.
He utilized his garden as a classroom, and relied heavily on donations to survive. Aside from the occasional college party, Epicurus and his students lived mostly on bread and water.

Epicurus developed his philosophy with a practical aim in mind, and so employed the use of logic and rationality as a means to happiness, rather than as tools for uncovering the truth for truth’s sake.
Although Epicurus outlines a hedonistic ethic, it is a sophisticated theory that encourages moderation.
Just as important to the Epicurean ethic is a reduction of desires. If we want less, we will be happy with less.
Friendship was the highest human relationship for Epicurus because it provided security, tranquility, and pleasure.
Furthermore, he argued that death is nothing to be fearful about, because it does not concern us.
Imagine the eternity before your birth… the eternity of nothingness. That doesn’t seem scary; you didn’t experience that nothingness.
